items.title: Buddy Tate interviewed by Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 3, 1995
items.q: they went down with Bird, with Charlie Parker or somebody in there

ctx.x: See now we’re getting in to [sounds like] Otto King’s world.
Yeah, we just loved Red. You know, I think they went down there with Max [Roach], they went down with Bird, with Charlie Parker or somebody in there. They called him “Albino Red.”

I wanted to ask you a couple of other questions. Is jazz education today, is it up to the task, or were there things that you were learning inside the big bands that are different or supersede or are better or are structured in a different way than jazz education today?

items.title: 56706_Buddy Tate oral history interview
items.q: Then, of course, he continued to play. I mean, we'd jam down there at night and he was playing

ctx.x: But still, I didn't ever get him. He didn't ever forget that. He always remembered me trying to get him in the band. And I used to have my wife -- I used to tell him to come up to the house. We didn't call, you know, like our cooking "soul food" then. We called it "down home," you know. I say, "Come on up to the house and I'll fix you a down home meal. And I'll have my wife to do it." So he says, "Okay." I says, "What do you want?" He says, "Well, you know what I like, anything." So he would come up there, this…

Then, of course, he continued to play. I mean, we'd jam down there at night and he was playing -- by then, he was playing what he wanted -- his style then, you know, but it hadn't really caught on with the people.
The bebop thing wasn't really such a tremendous revolution?
